strengths: EA-KD offers a simple, practical mechanism for improving vision model compression. Its weighting rule uses existing teacher and student predictions, introduces no auxiliary trainable module, and applies to both logit-based and feature-based distillation.

The experimental coverage is substantial: seven teacher–student pairs and seven distillation frameworks on CIFAR-100, alongside Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet, transformer-to-CNN transfer, and COCO detection. Table 2 reports an average improvement of 0.56 percentage points; gains of 0.76 points for ImageNet KD and 0.81/1.68 AP for COCO KD provide useful evidence beyond CIFAR-100.

The paper includes temperature and component ablations, a DKD hyperparameter sweep, runtime comparisons, and repeated-run statistics for EA variants. The supplement also compares against the closely related WTTM method and extends detection experiments to DKD.

The central formulation is clear and easy to implement. Relevant datasets and competing methods are cited, and a code repository is provided. The additional language-model experiments suggest potential applicability beyond vision.
weaknesses: The main experimental concern is that adaptive sample weighting is confounded with changing the overall distillation strength. Equations (12)–(14) use weights without normalizing their mean, thereby changing both the relative importance of samples and the balance between distillation and supervision. Section 4.1 even reduces the MLD+LS coefficient from 9 to 4. Controls using mean-normalized weights or constant weights matched to their average, alongside comparably tuned baseline coefficients, are needed to establish the claimed mechanism. The DKD beta sweep is useful but does not fully resolve this confound.

The distinctive contribution beyond existing teacher-uncertainty weighting is not convincingly isolated. In Table 9, adding student entropy improves teacher-only weighting by 0.32, 0.18, and 0.08 points for KD, MLD, and MLD+LS, respectively, and slightly reduces FCFD accuracy. These ablations lack uncertainty estimates. EA-TTM exceeds WTTM by only 0.03–0.19 points in Table A1, so the claimed superiority of dynamic weighting needs stronger evidence.

The explanatory claims exceed what the analysis establishes. Equations (5)–(7) correctly compare extreme teacher distributions against a uniformly initialized student, but smaller KL divergence for an already matched distribution does not establish a general harmful bias throughout training. The analogous claim connecting feature magnitude, MSE, and low entropy is unsupported. Predictive entropy can also reflect ambiguity or unreliable teacher predictions; the t-SNE visualizations do not establish that high-entropy samples necessarily contain more useful transferable knowledge.

Uncertainty in the baseline comparisons limits confidence in the smaller gains. Appendix C reports standard deviations for EA variants but relies on published baseline means. Matched baseline reruns would help distinguish improvements of roughly 0.1–0.3 points from seed variation or implementation differences, particularly for the strongest existing methods.

Several implementation details remain insufficiently specified in the manuscript: whether gradients propagate through student entropy, how detection predictions are aggregated into sample weights, and how token entropies produce sequence-level weights. Differentiating through student entropy introduces an additional gradient term, making this particularly relevant to reproducing and interpreting the method. Together with the missing controls, these concerns leave a slight preference for rejection despite the promising empirical breadth.
